name: Hannah Arendt
summary: Arendt was a political theorist who analysed totalitarianism and defended a republican politics of plurality, public freedom and citizen participation. She favoured federated councils over party rule, constitutional limits on majorities and the separation of powers, criticized both capitalism and state socialism for expropriating the masses, and opposed a sovereign Jewish state in favour of an Arab-Jewish federation.

notes: Single pass under rules 5 (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-12). All 26 of her books in the local reference library are cited or declined. Answers rest on her own words; as a theorist and journalist she held no office, so there is no record to weigh. Her positions on workers' councils are split: she championed political councils as a new form of government but judged workers' councils a failure as managers of factories, and in 1970 described councils leading up to a parliament, so workers-councils and organic-representation stay null. In the 1964 Gaus interview she said she was 'old-fashioned' and thought some occupations unbecoming for women, a personal remark that settles no statement on law or rights. Themes searched in her books: economy (property, expropriation, welfare state, unions, automation, consumption), government (councils, parties, representation, Senate, Supreme Court, plebiscites, majority rule, executive power, Watergate), world (sovereignty, world government, international courts, European federation, Zionism, Arab refugees, Vietnam), liberty (civil disobedience, segregation, surveillance, death penalty), society (education, religion, race, assimilation), technology (space, science, automation). Ecology, health care, taxation, drugs, sexuality, abortion and most technology statements found nothing in her writings.
